source: SEP Classical Logic
finding: Classical logic fixes syntax, a deductive system and model-theoretic semantics. Soundness: what is derivable is entailed. Completeness (Godel 1930): every consistent set of sentences is satisfiable.
numbers: Theorem 18 soundness; Theorem 20 completeness; Corollary 22 compactness; Theorems 25-26 downward and upward Lowenheim-Skolem. Read first 100,000 of 124,709 characters.
quote: If Γ is consistent, then Γ is satisfiable.
limits: The part read does not name Church, Cook, Gentzen or Tarski. First-order languages cannot pin down model size.
agent_relevance: Treat 'derivable' and 'true in all models' as the same thing for first-order rules. A contradiction check on stated rules (S4/S8) is a satisfiability question.

source: Wikipedia: Godel's completeness theorem
finding: Godel proved completeness in his 1929 Vienna thesis and published a shorter version in 1930. Henkin's model-existence proof (JSL 14, 1949) and Hasenjaeger's 1953 simplification are the modern route. The original proof used the Hilbert-Ackermann system.
numbers: 1929 thesis; 1930 Monatshefte paper; Henkin 1949; Hasenjaeger 1953. For countable languages completeness and compactness are equivalent to weak Konig's lemma; for arbitrary languages to the ultrafilter lemma.
limits: Secondary source. Neither theorem has a fully effective proof (the model construction is not recursive).
agent_relevance: Completeness says a proof exists if the claim is valid. It does not say a program can find it. Do not read 'complete' as 'always decidable'.

source: Wikipedia: Entscheidungsproblem (Church 1936, Turing 1936-37)
finding: Hilbert and Ackermann posed the decision problem in 1928. Church (1936, lambda calculus) and Turing (1936-37, halting problem) showed no algorithm decides first-order validity. Some fragments are decidable: Bernays-Schonfinkel (1928), the Ackermann class (1928), exists* forall^2 exists* (Godel, Schutte, Kalmar). Others are undecidable, e.g. forall^3 exists.
numbers: Church presented 19 April 1935, published 1936. Turing received 28 May 1936, Proc. LMS series 2 vol 42 (1936-7), corrections vol 43 (1937).
limits: The page does not state semi-decidability explicitly. Fragment list is partial.
agent_relevance: A first-order consistency check can run forever. The scaffold needs a timeout and a three-way answer: proved, refuted, unknown (budget out).

source: Wikipedia: Cook-Levin theorem
finding: Propositional satisfiability is NP-complete. Cook published it in 1971 (STOC, pp. 151-158); Levin in 1973 for search problems. Many practical SAT instances are still solved by heuristics.
numbers: Cook 1971; Levin 1973 (Probl. Inf. Transm. 9(3), 115-116).
limits: The page does not cover coNP-completeness of validity or CDCL solver scale, so those are not claimed from it.
agent_relevance: Propositional checking is decidable but worst-case hard. Put a budget on the solver call and treat timeout as 'unknown', not 'consistent'.

source: SEP Gottlob Frege
finding: Frege's Begriffsschrift (1879) is the start of modern formal logic. Russell's letter of 16 June 1902 showed a contradiction in Basic Law V of the Grundgesetze, not in the 1879 system.
numbers: Begriffsschrift 1879; Russell letter 16 June 1902. Read first 100,000 of 127,435 characters.
limits: The part read gives no detail of the 1879 axioms, rules or completeness status, so none is claimed.
agent_relevance: A natural-looking rule set can be inconsistent (Basic Law V). This is the historic case for a mechanical contradiction check on any rule list we write.

source: Han et al. (2022/2024) FOLIO: Natural Language Reasoning with First-Order Logic
finding: FOLIO is a human-written set of reasoning problems with parallel first-order-logic annotations checked by an inference engine. It also gives an NL-to-FOL translation task. Strong models stay far from solved.
numbers: 1,430 conclusions over 487 premise sets. Test majority baseline 38.5% (87 true, 78 false, 61 unknown). Prose numbers: LLaMA-13B 33.63%, LLaMA-70B 43.97%, text-davinci-002 49.53%, GPT-3.5 58.34%, Flan-T5-Large 65.7% (best fine-tuned). Logic-LM and DetermLR gave more than 13 points over few-shot GPT-4; LINC about 9 points.
limits: Table columns are garbled in the PDF text, so only numbers stated in prose are used. Exact GPT-4 rows not read.
agent_relevance: FOLIO is a real test of turning English rules into logic and checking them. Raw few-shot models are weak here.

source: Han et al. (2024) FOLIO: NL-to-FOL translation results
finding: Models write syntactically valid first-order logic almost always when shown examples, but the meaning is often wrong: the formulas fail when run through the inference engine.
numbers: Table 5: GPT-3.5-Turbo zero-shot syntactic validity 68.4, execution accuracy 50.4; few-shot 93.3 and 56.0. GPT-4 zero-shot 86.1 and 51.7; few-shot 93.9 and 63.8. Table 6 (WikiLogic vs HybLogic): GPT-4 NL-FOL execution accuracy 75.43 vs 53.10.
limits: Execution accuracy compares inference-engine labels, not formula equality. One prompt set.
agent_relevance: Valid syntax is not correct meaning. A formalisation step needs a semantic check, not just a parse check.

source: Saparov & He (2023, ICLR) Language Models are Greedy Reasoners (PrOntoQA)
finding: Synthetic first-order worlds let the authors parse chain-of-thought into proofs. InstructGPT/GPT-3 take mostly valid single steps but fail at proof planning: when several valid steps exist they pick misleading ones and do not search.
numbers: 5-hop fictional ontology: 93.2% of steps strictly valid, 2.4% broadly valid, 5.9% invalid (as printed). 1 and 3 hops handled well; 5-hop top-down falls to chance. Only text-davinci-002 beats chance. 400 examples per setting.
quote: LLMs are quite capable of making correct individual deduction steps
limits: Old GPT-3 family models. Synthetic, simple modus-ponens ontologies. Cause of the 001 vs 002 gap not found.
agent_relevance: Local inference is fine; global search is the weak part. Let code pick which rule to apply next and let the model apply one step.

source: Saparov & He (2023) PrOntoQA: world knowledge and traversal order
finding: With a 'true' ontology the model does much better and does not degrade from 3 to 5 hops, because it skips hops with real-world knowledge. Fictional and false ontologies give similar, lower accuracy. Context order (top-down vs bottom-up) matters more as hops grow.
numbers: Fictional vs false ontology comparable (false slightly worse); true ontology clearly better. The first non-canonical step in wrong proofs is most often a strictly-valid misleading step.
quote: Evidently, the model's reasoning is heavily reliant on real-world knowledge
limits: Bar-chart values not extracted as numbers. One model for the main results.
agent_relevance: When logic must hold against what is plausible, test on made-up predicates so memory cannot rescue a bad inference (G3).

source: Clark, Tafjord & Richardson (2020) Transformers as Soft Reasoners over Language (RuleTaker)
finding: Fine-tuned transformers answer true/false questions over facts and rules written in English with high accuracy, including on deeper chains than seen in training, and transfer to hand-written rulebases.
numbers: About 99% in-distribution; 95%+ on deeper depths when trained on lower depth; ParaRules paraphrased 98%; zero-shot hand-authored sets 90%+ in all but one case (one set 66%).
limits: Rules are simple Datalog-like with negation as failure, not full first-order logic. Training data come from the same generator.
agent_relevance: Models can emulate small rule engines but this is learned, not guaranteed. The scaffold should still call a real checker for anything that matters.

source: Tafjord, Dalvi Mishra & Clark (2021) ProofWriter
finding: A generative model iterated one inference step at a time produces proofs that reflect real model decisions. Proof correctness beats PRover by about 9 points absolute on RuleTaker and generalises to unseen depths and out-of-domain sets. It also does abduction (propose a missing fact).
numbers: Abstract: +9% absolute proof correctness. Hand-authored sets: All-At-Once 84.5%, PRover 80.5%, iterative 97.0% (adjacent table text). Answer accuracy around 99% at all depths.
limits: Some figures come from garbled table text; the triple is read from adjacent lines. Synthetic theories.
agent_relevance: One-step-at-a-time derivation (forward chaining) is more reliable than writing the whole proof at once. Matches 'model fills one slot, code decides next'.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: GPT-4 accuracy
finding: Translate to logic with the LLM, run a symbolic solver, interpret the result. With GPT-4 it beats Standard and CoT on 4 of 5 datasets; it loses to CoT on PrOntoQA.
numbers: GPT-4 Standard / CoT / Logic-LM: PrOntoQA 77.40 / 98.79 / 83.20; ProofWriter 52.67 / 68.11 / 79.66; FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33 / 75.25 / 87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33 / 35.06 / 43.04.
limits: About 600 examples per dataset; temperature 0; unexecutable cases fall back to CoT, which mixes the two methods. Early 2023 GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Solver delegation helps most where reasoning is non-linear (hypothesis, elimination), little where it is simple chaining. Use a solver at S4/S8 when the problem is of that kind.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: GPT-3.5 and self-refinement
finding: Average gain 39.2% over standard and 18.4% over CoT with GPT-3.5. Self-refinement from solver error messages raises the share of formulas that run, with small accuracy gains.
numbers: ChatGPT Standard / CoT / Logic-LM: FOLIO 45.09 / 57.35 / 62.74; ProofWriter 35.50 / 49.17 / 58.33. GPT-4 FOLIO executable rate 79.9% to 85.8% after refinement; AR-LSAT 32.6% to 39.8%.
limits: Execution rate measures grammar, not meaning; accuracy of executable samples is the real quality. AR-LSAT executable rate is low (32.6% for GPT-4).
agent_relevance: Real solver error text is a good revision signal (G2). Many formalisations never run, so the agent needs a fallback path.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: FOLIO
finding: LLM translates to FOL, Prover9 checks, 10-way majority vote over the translations. On FOLIO it helps small and mid models but not GPT-4, where it ties CoT.
numbers: StarCoder+ 15.5B: LINC 56.0% vs closest baseline 41.8%. GPT-4 FOLIO: CoT 75.3% vs LINC 72.5%, McNemar p = 0.58. LINC predicts Uncertain 57% vs CoT 41%; precision on True/False 93% vs 81%; recall 60% vs 75%.
limits: FOL syntax errors in generated formulas: 38% StarCoder+, 24% GPT-3.5, 13% GPT-4. Information lost in translation (one fused symbol, NaziGermanPolitician) caused missed deductions.
agent_relevance: Formal checking is sound but lossy: it says 'unknown' when the translation dropped something. Treat 'unknown' as a signal to re-read the text, not a verdict.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: ProofWriter balanced subset
finding: On synthetic ProofWriter the solver route is far better than CoT and holds at deep proofs where baselines collapse.
numbers: LINC mean accuracy GPT-3.5 96.4%, GPT-4 98.3%. Abstract: StarCoder+ with LINC beats GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 CoT by 38 and 10 points; GPT-4 LINC 26 points above CoT. GPT-3.5 with LINC near perfect at all depths, baselines near chance beyond depth 1.
limits: Authors give two reasons it may not generalise: ProofWriter is synthetic with short sentences, and baselines face a distribution shift to larger premise sets.
agent_relevance: Gain is largest on clean synthetic rule text. Expect smaller gains on messy real rules.

source: Ye, Chen, Dillig & Durrett (2023) SATLM
finding: Have the model write a declarative spec (constraints) and let a SAT/SMT solver (Z3) answer. It beats imperative program-aided LMs and CoT on logic and constraint problems.
numbers: code-davinci-002 greedy, SATLM vs CoT: ProofWriter 99.7 vs 80.1; CLUTRR 68.3 vs 40.8; LSAT 35.0 vs 23.5; BoardgameQA 79.4 vs 60.7; ALGEBRA 77.5 vs 53.6; GSM-SYS 69.4 vs 46.5. GSM: 71.8 vs program-aided 72.7 (on par). SATLM over PROGLM gains p < 0.05 by bootstrap.
limits: Old model (code-davinci-002). The solver is correct only relative to the parsed spec.
agent_relevance: A declarative rule list plus solver suits an S4 contradiction test: write constraints, ask 'satisfiable?'.

source: Lyu et al. (2023) Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Two stages: LM translates to a symbolic chain, a deterministic solver answers. The chain is then a true record of the answer, and it beat standard CoT on 9 of 10 benchmarks.
numbers: Relative gains: 6.3% math word problems, 3.4% planning, 5.5% multi-hop QA, 21.4% relational inference.
limits: Only the abstract and first page were read. Benchmarks are mostly not pure logic.
agent_relevance: Supports the schema rule that written reasoning is not a reliable record of what decided the answer; use a solver chain.

source: Chen, Chi, Wang & Zhou (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with LLMs
finding: Reordering the same premises changes deduction accuracy a lot. Best when order matches the proof (forward); worse as order deviates. GPT-4-turbo prefers backward over shuffled; PaLM 2-L is worst at backward.
numbers: Permuting premise order can cause a drop of over 30%. GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L lose up to 20-30 points; Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo fall from over 65% to below 25%. R-GSM: GPT-4-turbo 94.1% to 85.0%.
quote: LLMs are surprisingly brittle to the ordering of the premises
limits: Simple rule-chaining task. 2025 reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Logic is order-invariant but models are not. Shuffle premise order as a mutation test in S8 (G3) and flag any change in verdict.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Premise Order: error types
finding: The most common error is fact hallucination: the model invents an unproven fact to complete a step when the next rule is not yet usable. Distracting rules enlarge the order effect.
numbers: GPT-4-turbo, 12 relevant rules, no distractors: forward order 96.5% correct; other orders 76.0-84.5% in the printed table.
limits: Percentages read from table text; the order-parameter row labels are partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Check each derived fact against a named premise; unsupported facts are the dominant failure.

source: Parmar et al. (2024) LogicBench
finding: 25 patterns over propositional, first-order and non-monotonic logic, one inference rule per question. Models do poorly on negation and rules like modus tollens, and sometimes ignore context.
numbers: ChatGPT 48.04% and GPT-4 63.98% average yes-accuracy on propositional logic. GPT-4 about 85% on hypothetical syllogism but about 59% on modus tollens (propositional). Humans above 85% (as reported).
limits: Template-based questions; negation effects may partly be dataset style. Chain-of-thought throughout.
agent_relevance: Modus tollens and negation are known weak spots; the contradiction checker should not rely on model judgement for them.

source: Patel et al. (2024) Multi-LogiEval
finding: Accuracy falls steadily as the number of reasoning steps rises, across propositional and first-order logic.
numbers: Mean over models: propositional 85.42 (depth 1) to 42.96 (depth 5); first-order 83.21 to 32.96. GPT-4 propositional 89.17 to 66.67; first-order 83.85 to 66.67. Abstract: about 68% at depth 1 to about 43% at depth 5. Orca-13B depth-5 first-order 6.67.
limits: Zero-shot CoT; 2023 models. Depth-5 sets are small (110 items).
agent_relevance: Break long deductions into depth-1 steps checked one at a time.

source: Qi et al. (2025, ICLR) ProverGen / ProverQA
finding: LLM-written stories checked by symbolic provers give a first-order benchmark where strong models still fail on hard cases. Fine-tuning Llama3.1-8B on its training set helped.
numbers: CoT: GPT-4o ProverQA easy 94.20, medium 79.40, hard 50.00; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 95.20 / 83.60 / 56.40. Standard prompting GPT-4o hard 46.20. ProntoQA with CoT: GPT-4o 100.00, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 99.20.
limits: 2024 non-reasoning models. Reasoning-budget models not tried.
agent_relevance: Older public sets are saturated; difficulty is deep proofs with distractors. Test the scaffold on hard cases.

source: Chen, Zhang & Tao (2025) JustLogic
finding: A synthetic deductive benchmark with random truth values, so prior knowledge does not help. Reasoning models reach or pass the human average; none reach the ceiling.
numbers: Human average 73.0%, human ceiling 100%. DeepSeek R1 80.9%, OpenAI o1 72.9%, GPT-4o 65.6%. Random 33.3%. Zero-shot Llama3-8B 49.8%, Llama3-70B 53.1%.
limits: Human sample details not extracted. Random truth values are unnatural for real use.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models are near the human average on pure deduction, so the scaffold's value is in checking, not raw deduction.

source: Chen, Zhang & Tao (2025) JustLogic: prior-knowledge test
finding: FOLIO and LogiQA 2.0 contain questions answerable without the context, so high scores may overstate logic skill. ProofWriter and CLUTRR are nearly knowledge-free.
numbers: Authors report non-trivial no-context gaps above random for FOLIO and LogiQA 2.0 and small gaps for ProofWriter and CLUTRR. Exact values (Table 4) not copied.
limits: Exact numbers for other benchmarks not extracted.
agent_relevance: FOLIO scores overstate pure logic; judge the scaffold on knowledge-free items too.

source: Synthesis: Church, Turing, Cook limits for a checker
finding: Three limits together define what a checker can promise: first-order validity is only semi-decidable, propositional satisfiability is NP-complete, and completeness says proofs exist but is non-constructive.
numbers: Dates: Hilbert-Ackermann 1928; Godel 1929/1930; Church 1936; Turing 1936-37; Cook 1971; Levin 1973.
limits: Synthesis of lines a02-a04 only; no new source.
agent_relevance: Design the verifier with three outcomes and a budget: refuted, proved, unknown.
